column4: God leaves the mountains قَاعًا صَفْصَفًا, the bare level plain that most directly matches the section's account of a people made into flat ground.
The level field of 20:106 has neither bend nor rise; this ayah supplies the visible content of the section's "none set apart" reading of leveling.
Those who rejected the messenger wish لَوْ تُسَوَّىٰ بِهِمُ الْأَرْضُ; the same sewwā root turns human distinction into earth-level indistinction.
نُسَوِّيَ بَنَانَهُ uses the same root for the exact re-forming of fingertips, making explicit the section's claim that minute formation and annihilating leveling belong to one power.
Ṣāliḥ names both sides of Thamūd's terrain: palaces on its plains and houses carved from mountains, the raised works the section sees reduced to the plane beneath them.
Thamūd جَابُوا الصَّخْرَ بِالْوَادِ, cutting rock in the valley; this is the monumental mountain-building that gives their later leveling its force.
They carved houses from mountains ءَامِنِينَ; their felt security inside elevated stone is precisely what the section's ruin scene overturns.
After the quake, Thamūd lie جَاثِمِينَ in their own dwelling: the narrative itself shows the people pressed down where their built life stood.
كَأَن لَّمْ يَغْنَوْا فِيهَا makes Thamūd's settled presence disappear as though they had never inhabited the place, completing the section's image of a civilization erased to ground.
The single cry makes them كَهَشِيمِ الْمُحْتَظِرِ, crushed enclosure-straw; it is the Quran's most concrete analogue for the section's people spread flat like a trampled field.
They cannot rise and cannot help themselves after 51:44; inability to stand renders the secondary tahā sense of being struck and stretched on the ground.
فَتِلْكَ بُيُوتُهُمْ خَاوِيَةً بِمَا ظَلَمُوا points to their emptied, fallen houses and expressly ties the ruin to wrongdoing, just as the section ties leveling to sin.
The immense barrier becomes دَكَّاءَ when God's promise comes; a divinely enabled construction is made level by the same Lord, a close structural parallel to the image's two works of one power.
حَتَّىٰ إِذَا سَاوَىٰ بَيْنَ الصَّدَفَيْنِ uses the s-w-y root while building an elevated barrier level with the two cliffs; 18:98 then reverses that construction into leveling.
Earth and mountains are lifted and crushed دَكَّةً وَاحِدَةً; their heights become one under a single blow, matching both flatness and equality in the section.
دُكَّتِ الْأَرْضُ دَكًّا دَكًّا stages the earth itself being pounded flat, a direct nonlexical formulation of fe-sewwāhā.
God makes the mountain دَكًّا and Moses falls down stunned; mountain and person together enact the section's linked senses of leveling and being struck to earth.
Mountains are removed, earth stands exposed, and no person is left out of the gathering; the ayah joins a bare plane to the section's concern with nobody being set apart.
The question concerns the mountains and the answer says God will scatter them completely; it identifies what God turns into the level field described in 20:106-107.
God attacks a building from its foundations and its roof falls upon its occupants; raised shelter becoming the agent of collapse closely matches the fate of Thamūd's refuges.
Wrongdoing towns become خَاوِيَةٌ عَلَىٰ عُرُوشِهَا beside an abandoned well and a lofty palace; ruin, habitation, and the high building meet exactly as in the section.
People think their fortresses will protect them, but their houses are demolished by their own hands and the believers'; this makes explicit the failed refuge implicit in Thamūd's secure rock houses.
A town lies خَاوِيَةٌ عَلَىٰ عُرُوشِهَا and the same episode demonstrates bones being assembled and clothed; ruin and exact re-formation are placed under one power as in the section.
A building on a crumbling bank collapses with its builder; the ayah turns construction itself into a fall and contrasts it with the sound foundation named earlier in the verse.
The proud garden may become صَعِيدًا زَلَقًا, bare slippery ground; flourishing possession is reduced to a plane just as Thamūd's constructed landscape is leveled.
The garden's produce is destroyed and its trellises lie خَاوِيَةً عَلَىٰ عُرُوشِهَا; it supplies the collapsed built scene whose final ground-state 18:40 anticipates.
Thamūd hamstring the she-camel, عَقَرُوا النَّاقَةَ, and defiantly demand punishment; this is the first toppling from which the section reads their own toppling.
فَعَقَرُوهَا repeats the communal hamstringing and gives the three-day limit, setting the camel's fall directly before the people's destruction.
فَعَقَرُوهَا makes the camel's hamstringing the immediate act for which the people become regretful and are seized, preserving the section's two-stage fall.
One companion undertakes the act, فَعَقَرَ, while the ensuing punishment reaches the people; this sharpens the section's movement from one assailant to a community made one in consequence.
The blast seizes Thamūd's wrongdoers and leaves them جَاثِمِينَ in their homes, the same bodily ground-state highlighted through 7:78.
The cry takes the rock-house dwellers in the morning; after 15:82's claim of security, this ayah performs the sudden overthrow.
The punishment seizes them immediately after the camel is hamstrung, completing the section's causal passage from the animal's fall to the people's.
God states أَنَّا دَمَّرْنَاهُمْ وَقَوْمَهُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ; total destruction of the plotters and their people directly expresses the section's eradication and collective leveling.
Thamūd choose blindness after guidance and are seized by a humiliating thunderbolt because of what they earned, preserving both culpability and communal ruin.
They rebel against their Lord's command and the thunderbolt takes them while they look on; it supplies the blow whose bodily result is the inability to stand in 51:45.
وَثَمُودَ فَمَا أَبْقَىٰ says that no remainder of Thamūd was left, the clearest Quranic statement behind the section's "none separately spared" sense.
Thamūd are destroyed بِالطَّاغِيَةِ; the concise communal end names the same people and the overwhelming force that brings them low.
The she-camel is given to Thamūd as a visible sign and they wrong her; the ayah isolates the sign whose violation the section makes the hinge of reciprocal overthrow.
خَلَقَكَ فَسَوَّاكَ فَعَدَلَكَ joins creation, proportioning, and balance; it states directly the formative and equalizing face of the root used for the soul in the section.
الَّذِي خَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ makes creating and proportioning one divine act, a terse parallel to the formative sewwāhā side of the image.
From the clot God creates and فَسَوَّىٰ; within the same surah as the fingertip promise, the root again denotes exact human formation.
ثُمَّ سَوَّاهُ describes God's proportioning of the human before breathing spirit into him, directly paralleling the section's fashioned self.
The believer reminds his companion that God created him from dust and a drop, then سَوَّاكَ رَجُلًا; the root marks a person brought to finished form.
The messenger appears as بَشَرًا سَوِيًّا, a well-formed human; this distinct Quranic use of the root illuminates the section's "properly formed" branch.
God raises the sky's vault and فَسَوَّاهَا; the same root fashions the sky whose building stands beside the fashioned self in the surah's oaths.
فَسَوَّاهُنَّ سَبْعَ سَمَاوَاتٍ applies the root to ordering the heavens, extending the section's formation sense from the self to the cosmic structure.
God makes the earth a bed and the sky a building; this ayah reunites the spread earth and built heaven that precede the section's two uses of sewwā.
The earth is a settled place, the sky a structure, and human forms are made beautiful; all three elements of the section's created plane, building, and fitted person occur together.
The command to look at how the earth سُطِحَتْ presents the prepared flat surface that the section treats as the prior form of later leveling.
وَالْأَرْضَ بَعْدَ ذَٰلِكَ دَحَاهَا depicts the earth spread out, a close nonlexical parallel to ṭaḥāhā as an open plane.
At the end the earth is مُدَّتْ, stretched out; created extension becomes an eschatological scene of the plane, matching the section's movement from preparation to leveling.
The earth is shaken violently; this opens the sequence in which its mountains are pulverized and become scattered dust in 56:5-6.
The mountains are ground to powder, a direct enactment of raised mass losing every stable height before 56:6 disperses it.
The pulverized mountains become scattered dust, the final material state of the leveling begun in 56:4-5.
Each destroyed people is seized for its sin by storm, blast, earth, or flood; the ayah expressly unites culpability with differing divine acts of bringing societies down.
The people of ʿĀd lie fallen like hollow palm trunks, a bodily landscape parallel to Thamūd left prostrate on their own ground.
فَهَلْ تَرَىٰ لَهُم مِّن بَاقِيَةٍ asks whether any remnant remains after 69:7, reinforcing the section's reading of totality rather than individual distinction.
The wind uproots people as though they were trunks of uprooted palms; bodily felling and eradication parallel the section's joined senses of collapse and istiʾṣāl.
The barren wind leaves whatever it reaches كَالرَّمِيمِ, decayed remains; it supplies another Quranic scene of destruction reducing a people and their world to spent material.
A wrongdoing town is made حَصِيدًا خَامِدِينَ, reaped and extinguished; the harvest image closely parallels Thamūd as crushed enclosure-straw.
A single cry leaves the town خَامِدُونَ, joining one decisive sound to collective stillness as in the accounts of Thamūd.
When the command comes, God saves Ṣāliḥ and those who believe with him; this sets the moral boundary around 11:67-68's communal leveling.
After the houses stand empty, God saves those who believed and were mindful; the ayah prevents "all made one" from erasing the distinction made within the same Thamūd account.
Believers who were mindful are saved from the thunderbolt of 41:17, explicitly separating them from the culpable community brought low.
The evildoers ask whether God will make them سَوَاءً with believers in life and death; this denied equality marks the limit of the section's equality-through-destruction reading.
The wind leaves nothing visible of ʿĀd except their dwellings; the surviving buildings form a precise counter-scene to Thamūd's houses themselves shown empty and ruined.
God does not destroy towns unjustly while their people are reformers; this is a direct boundary on the section's image of an entire settlement leveled for sin.
God saves those He wills and destroys the excessive; the paired outcomes clarify that one power does not entail an undifferentiated moral fate.
Ṣāliḥ presents God's she-camel as a sign, orders that she feed on God's earth, and warns against harming her; it supplies the charged animal and ground before the first toppling.
Ṣāliḥ calls her God's she-camel and warns that harm will bring near punishment, making explicit the causal symmetry developed by the section.
The camel has her allotted drink and the people theirs; the measured sharing makes her violation a concrete breach rather than an incidental animal death.
Ṣāliḥ warns them not to touch her with harm lest a tremendous day's punishment seize them; 26:157-158 carry that warned reversal out.
God sends the camel as a test and commands watchful patience; this frames the act of hamstringing as the decisive communal trial.
Water is divided and each drinking turn attended; this supplies the measured order that the act in 54:29 breaks.
Ṣāliḥ says God produced Thamūd from the earth and settled them in it; their earth-derived, earth-building life sharpens their final reduction to that ground.
The question "Will you be left secure in what is here?" exposes the permanence assumed by the people who carve enduring homes.
They carve mountain houses with skill or exultation; this close parallel to 15:82 adds human confidence and craft to the structures later unable to save them.
What the rock-house dwellers had earned avails them nothing after the cry, naming the failure of accumulated works to resist leveling.
Thamūd are told to enjoy themselves only for a time; the bounded respite prepares the rebellion and collapse of 51:44-45.
Thamūd deny the warnings; the ayah identifies the collective stance answered by the camel test and single cry later in the passage.
Thamūd and ʿĀd deny the Striking Calamity; it gives the shared act of rejection whose distinct bodily destructions follow.
God spreads the earth and places firm mountains in it; the pairing of extension with height supplies the very topography later turned into an unbroken plane.
God extends the earth and sets mountains and rivers upon it; this differentiates the plane and its raised features before the leveling image removes such distinction.
The earth is spread and firm mountains cast into it, another direct formulation of the extended ground presupposed by the section.
وَالْأَرْضَ فَرَشْنَاهَا presents God as the one who spread the earth, matching the speaker and act behind the section's prior plane.
God makes the earth a carpet for humankind; the usable expanse parallels the open flat-land sense attached to ṭaḥā.
The earth is made a resting spread, a compact parallel to the section's prepared level ground.
God makes the earth a cradle and lays paths through it; its fitted habitability supplies the constructive face of the ground later leveled in the same surah.
God makes the earth a cradle and places ways within it, another scene of the ground deliberately fitted before human building.
On the earth God fixes mountains, blesses it, measures its provisions, and makes them سَوَاءً for those who ask; the root's equality sense appears within an ordered earthly landscape.
The layered heavens show no تَفَاوُت, no disparity in the Merciful's creation; this states in other words the fitted, non-disjointed order conveyed by formative sewwā.
God creates the heavens and earth and makes human forms beautiful; cosmic construction and finished human form again belong to the same agent.
Humanity is created فِي أَحْسَنِ تَقْوِيمٍ, a nonlexical parallel to the self being brought into a sound, balanced form.
After recalling human creation and proportioning, the passage asks whether that maker can revive the dead; it states the power inference the section draws from exact formation.
The denier presents decayed bones and forgets his own creation; his objection gives the resurrection-denial setting behind the section's fingertip example.
The answer says the one who originated the bones first will revive them, explicitly joining original formation to re-formation after destruction.
Earth and mountains convulse and the mountains become a heap of loose sand; stable height collapses toward the section's level-ground end.
The mountains are blown away, removing the raised features that distinguish the landscape from a plain.
The mountains are set moving and become a mirage, turning apparent solidity into absence.
The mountains are set in motion, an eschatological removal of the heights that structure ordinary ground.
The mountains move away completely, another Quranic dissolution of the elevated landscape.
Mountains become like fluffed wool, a material unmaking comparable to the section's hard-built world reduced to loose remains.
Mountains become like dyed wool, carrying the same reversal from weight and height to dispersed fiber.
ʿĀd build a monument on every height in play; the elevated building supplies a comparative scene of a powerful people investing in conspicuous height.
They take great structures as though they might live forever; the imagined permanence directly contrasts with a built people being erased.
ʿĀd deny their messenger and are destroyed, completing the construction-to-destruction comparison opened by 26:128-129.
Earlier peoples worked and developed the earth more powerfully, yet wronged themselves after messengers came; built abundance therefore gives no immunity from the moral cause of ruin.
Former peoples were stronger and left greater traces in the earth, but God seized them for their sins; this closely restates monumental power followed by culpable erasure.
Stronger generations ranged through lands seeking escape, yet found none; strength and reach fail as refuge just as Thamūd's stone works do.
Self-indulgent towns are destroyed and their dwellings remain scarcely inhabited, paralleling the section's civilization reduced to empty habitation.
Later people walk through the dwellings of generations God destroyed; remaining houses become evidence of inhabitants removed.
The destruction of earlier generations whose dwellings are still traversed makes ruined habitation an admonitory sign, as Thamūd's houses are in the section.
Well-established generations with rain and rivers are destroyed for their sins and replaced; provision, settlement, and culpable removal form the same arc.
A people more firmly established than the addressees lose the benefit of hearing, sight, and hearts when they reject God's signs; establishment cannot prevent disappearance.
Midian's denial brings the quake and leaves them جَاثِمِينَ in their dwelling, repeating outside the Thamūd story the exact posture of a people struck to ground.
The quake leaves Midian جَاثِمِينَ in their home, a repeated Quranic formula for communal collapse within the inhabited center.
The blast leaves Shuʿayb's wrongdoers جَاثِمِينَ in their homes, confirming that the posture developed in the section is a recurring image of judgment.
God makes the top of Lot's towns their bottom; the literal reversal of high and low is a close companion to reducing raised habitation to ground.
The overturned towns have their highest part made lowest, another direct scene in which built elevation is divinely inverted.
The army is made like eaten straw, a compact parallel to Thamūd's reduction to crushed enclosure-straw in 54:31.
The owners' fruitful garden becomes like a field cut down overnight; cultivated abundance is abruptly reduced to a reaped surface.
